To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the oxygen isotope record is a mixed signal of deep-sea temperature changes and ice-volume changes.
the Cenozoïc δ 18 O deep-sea temperature curve is significantly colder than the Mg/Ca curve and the Pliocene cooling rate is much larger in δ 18 O than in Mg/Ca.

the Cenozo ic δ18O record is a mixed signal (ice-volume and temperature contribute equally to its variance) and that it is likely that the Pliocene cooling rate is significantly larger than that suggested by the Mg/Ca record.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the separation of the temperature and ice-volume signals in the benthic oxygen-isotope record.
the separation of the ice volume and temperature signals from the oxygen isotope record of benthic foram calcite.
the separation of the temperature and ice-volume signals in benthic δ 18O records.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Mg/Ca method is not a reliable measure for deep-sea temperatures.
the Cenozoicoxygen isotope record of deep-sea cores reflects both deep-sea temperature fluctuations and fluctuations in Antarctic ice volume.
the δ 18O temperature curve is the most reliable temperature proxy for the Cenozic, and that the Mg/Ca proxy is a good indicator of temperature, but not a good indicator of ice volume.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the δ18O and Mg/Ca temperature records do not agree.
the Mg/Ca and the δ 18O temperature records for the last 65 Myr are not consistent with each other and that the δ 18Os signal is a mixed signal.
the Mg/Ca method is a good method to determine deep-sea temperatures, but that the method of comparing the δ 18O and Mg/Ca signals is not a reliable method to determine ice-volume.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the oxygen-isotope temperature curve is a much better indicator of the deep-sea temperature than the Mg/Ca curve.
a simple ice-sheet model, forced by a corrected deep-ocean oxygen isotope record, is able to reproduce the main features of the Cenozoicocean temperature record.
the δ 18O record from benthics provides a reliable record of temperature change in the deep ocean.
